newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German orders drop dampens growth prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German orders drop dampens growth prospects.

text.p: German industry orders slowed sharply in September, data showed on Tuesday, but analysts said that fears of recovery choking off could be allayed by a likely upward revision later.
Industrial orders fell by 3.6 percent in September against August, while the August figure was revised down to show a modest gain of 0.1 percent on the previous month.
"We had expected some weakness in the new orders data, but the reported slump by 3.6 percent is far beyond all forecasts," Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt wrote in a commentary.
Economist Holger Schmieding at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt called the number "disappointing", but echoed a warning by the Economics Ministry that the numbers would be revised up later.
Initial September data are seen as particularly unreliable by economists because companies are usually late in reporting figures after the summer break.

Matthias Haffner of Barclays de Zoete Wedd dismissed a slowdown in export orders as mainly linked to erratic factors. But a tailing off in domestic orders in the third quarter against the second quarter was more worrying.
"We expect an upward revision, but I cannot see that we will end up with a positive number for September," he said.
Most economists agree the German economy should grow by at least one percent this year, and their forecasts tend to be in line with official expectations of 2.5 percent growth in 1997.
But if the setback in orders, which followed the release on Monday of weak industrial production figures, is confirmed then there may be cause to take another look at recovery prospects.
"It is all getting tighter. If there is another bad number next month then we will have to rethink," Haffner said.
Commerzbank's Peter Pietsch agreed: "This is a very disappointing number and is definitely a dampener on optimistic expectations," he told Reuters.
Fahrinkrug of UBS said the data would not have an impact on third quarter gross domestic product growth, but would create a low basis for the fourth quarter and beyond.
Economists said the data confirmed that a sharp jump in growth in this year's second quarter was a catch-up following a winter downturn, and did not look sustainable.
"There are now mounting signs that the economy is not taking off in the way the second quarter GDP numbers had suggested," James Capel's Robert Prior-Wandesforde wrote.
"We stick to our view that Germany is likely to see something of a growth hump," he added in a note.

The industry orders data coincided with the release of the industry-based Federation of German Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) autumn survey of 25,000 companies, which found that businesses expected the recovery to continue, albeit slowly.

"Companies are still missing the certainty of a strong and lasting recovery," the DIHT said. The DIHT expects gross domestic product to grow by less than two percent next year -- below the official forecast.

A breakdown of the September figures, which are seasonally adjusted and based on volume, showed that orders were down in western Germany by 3.6 percent against August. In the former communist east, orders were down by 2.6 percent.
Foreign orders, which have been helping to lead Germany's recovery from a recession last winter, fell back by 4.1 percent in September after a gain of 2.4 percent in August.
Domestic orders slowed by 3.2 percent in September, the third month running, after a fall of 1.4 percent in August.
But a two-month comparison of the latest two months against a year earlier still showed foreign orders up a robust 6.6 percent, while domestic orders were down by 4.3 percent.
